# Residual-covariance normalization: simplex products and an exact obstruction

This note changes the normalization of continuous cap normals. It proves
that the Euclidean abnormality of a nonregular simplex product disappears
under residual-covariance normalization. It also gives an actual
non-product convex body for which abnormality persists at the minimum
feasible budget in that normalization. Neither assertion is an OC proof.

## 1. The residual covariance and allowed transformations

Let the mixed source have positive full-dimensional fibers in R^d,
`d>=1`, total mass `M`, and associated probability law `(Z,X)`.
Zero-volume fibers, if present, do not enter this probability law. Put

`V=Cov(Z)`, `C_XZ=Cov(X,Z)`.

Choose a regression matrix `B` satisfying `B V=C_XZ`, and define

`R=X-E X-B(Z-E Z)`, `Sigma=Cov(R)`.

Such a matrix exists, even if `V` is singular: if `v in ker V`, then
`v dot(Z-E Z)=0` almost surely, so `C_XZ v=0`. One choice is
`B=C_XZ V^+`. Any two choices give the same residual almost surely.
For `n=0`, this is simply `R=X-E X`.

The matrix `Sigma` is positive definite. Indeed the law of total
covariance expresses it as the sum of `E Cov(X|Z)` and a positive
semidefinite matrix. Every positive full-dimensional fiber has positive
definite conditional covariance, so the first summand is positive
definite.

Normalize every cap margin

`L(z,x)=a dot z+u dot x-b`

by `u^T Sigma u=1`. The matrix `Sigma` is fixed while cap parameters
are varied; this is not a variation of the source body.

Consider an allowed change of coordinates

`z'=U z+h`, `x'=A x+D z+e`,

where `U` is unimodular, `h` is integer, and `A` is invertible. The
regressor space generated by the base coordinates is unchanged. A
valid transformed regression matrix is `(A B+D)U^(-1)`, and its
residual is `R'=A R`. Consequently

`Sigma'=A Sigma A^T`.

Writing the same affine margin in the new coordinates gives

`u'=A^(-T)u`, `a'=U^(-T)(a-D^T u')`,
`b'=b+a' dot h+u' dot e`.

Thus `u'^T Sigma' u'=u^T Sigma u`, exactly. All fiber volumes, cap
masses, and hinges multiply by `Delta=|det A|`; normalized cap budgets
are unchanged. Regression shears alone have `Delta=1` and preserve
all these masses. Whitening by `A=Sigma^(-1/2)` transforms this
normalization into the Euclidean one for the transformed source.

The normal stress transforms consistently: its budget multipliers
`r_i` remain unchanged, while coverage and sphere multipliers multiply
by `Delta`; contacts are pushed forward and their simplex weights stay
the same. Mass and base equations cancel the extra affine terms in
the transformed continuous moment equation.

## 2. Covariance-normalized moment equation

Use the sphere equation `(u^T Sigma u-1)/2=0`. Its differential is
`Sigma u`. With objective multiplier `alpha_0`, the continuous equation
is therefore

`alpha_0 X_i+r_i X_i^s-sum_z eta_z q_zi+sigma_i Sigma u_i=0`.

The mass and integer equations are unchanged. Their Euler combination
with this equation gives `sigma_i=-alpha_0 Psi_i`, since
`u_i^T Sigma u_i=1`. Thus

`alpha_0 X_i+r_i X_i^s-sum_z eta_z q_zi
     =alpha_0 Psi_i Sigma u_i`.                       (1)

The same calculation holds for finite measures of actual saddle pairs.
There is no factorization of their contact moments in this statement.

## 3. Exact simplex covariance identities

Let `K` be a d-simplex with vertices `v_0,...,v_d`, centroid `g`,
centered vertices `w_j=v_j-g`, barycentric coordinates `lambda_j`,
and gradients `beta_j=grad lambda_j`. Uniform simplex moments give

`Sigma_K = [sum_j w_j w_j^T]/[(d+1)(d+2)]`.

For completeness, the barycentric second moments are
`E lambda_i^2=2/[(d+1)(d+2)]` and
`E lambda_i lambda_j=1/[(d+1)(d+2)]` for distinct indices; these follow
by integrating monomials on the standard simplex. Expanding
`X-g=sum lambda_j w_j` and using `sum w_j=0` yields the formula.

Since `beta_i dot w_j=delta_ij-1/(d+1)`, it follows exactly that

`Sigma_K beta_i=w_i/[(d+1)(d+2)]`,
`beta_i^T Sigma_K beta_i=d/[(d+1)^2(d+2)]`.              (2)

Write the common positive square root in (2) as `kappa`. The canonical
centroid vertex cap has normalized margin

`L_i=(lambda_i-1/(d+1))/kappa`, `u_i=beta_i/kappa`.

Its mass, centroid displacement, and hinge-to-mass ratio are

`c=gamma_d |K|`, `g_i-g=w_i/(d+1)`,
`Psi_i/c=d/[(d+1)^2 kappa]
        =sqrt(d(d+2))/(d+1)`.                         (3)

Indeed this cap is a copy of `K` scaled by `d/(d+1)` about `v_i`.
That proves its volume and centroid formulas; applying its affine
margin to its centroid gives the hinge-to-mass ratio. Equations
(2)--(3) imply the exact vector identity

`c(g_i-g)=Psi_i Sigma_K u_i`.                          (4)

## 4. Every simplex product admits a normal sharp-budget stress

Take `S={0,1}^n x K`, including `n=0`, put `m=2^n`, and use
`N=m(d+1)` caps. The residual covariance is `Sigma_K`, because `X`
and `Z` are independent. Tilt the canonical caps on each binary fiber
so that they are strictly empty on every other source fiber. This is
possible by the affine binary distance to that vertex. Each local
canonical family covers its entire continuous space: the barycentric
coordinates always sum to one, so some coordinate is at least
`1/(d+1)`.

The minimum feasible normalized cap budget is `gamma_d/m`. The
ordinary simplex centroid inequality gives its lower bound on any
cap covering a fiber centroid, and the displayed cover attains it.
At the prescribed cap count, the exact simplex equality classification
proved in `candidate 0e807db2bba0c137` gives its
canonical sharp-budget structure.

Set `alpha_0=1`, all `r_i=0`, and at every fiber use the unique contact
`g`, with weights `lambda_i=1/(d+1)` on its local caps and zero
elsewhere. These weights are balanced because all normalizing factors
`kappa` agree and `sum beta_i=0`. Set

`eta_z=(d+1)c`, `sigma_i=-Psi_i`.

Mass and base equations hold directly, and (4) proves the continuous
equations. Hence this is a normal stress with zero budget multipliers
for every simplex, regardless of its Euclidean shape. The canonical
sharp-budget hinge value in this normalization is

`M gamma_d sqrt(d(d+2))`.

## 5. The local compatibility condition for a different common covariance

Suppose a simplex fiber has an own canonical cap, its contact is its
centroid, and multiplied section moments from other fibers vanish.
Its own section has centroid `g` and density one. Eliminating the
mass equation from (1) shows that a positive objective multiplier
requires

`w_i/(d+1)
   =d Sigma beta_i/[(d+1)^2(beta_i^T Sigma beta_i)]`     (5)

for every local cap type. This condition holds for all types if and
only if `Sigma` is a positive scalar multiple of `Sigma_K`.

To prove necessity, put `v_i=Sigma_K^(1/2) beta_i` and
`T=Sigma_K^(-1/2) Sigma Sigma_K^(-1/2)`. Equation (2) converts (5)
into the assertion that each `v_i` is an eigenvector of the symmetric
matrix `T`. Distinct vectors have nonzero inner product:

`v_i dot v_j=-1/[(d+1)^2(d+2)]`, `i!=j`.

Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are
orthogonal. Thus all these eigenvalues agree. The `v_i` span R^d,
so `T` is scalar. Sufficiency follows immediately from (2); the scalar
factor cancels between the numerator and denominator in (5).

## 6. Exact non-product abnormality in dimension three

Let `n=1,d=2`, and put

`K_0=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)}`,
`K_1=diag(2,1/2) K_0`,
`C=conv(({0}xK_0) union ({1}xK_1))`.

This is a full-dimensional convex body in R^3. Its projection is
`[0,1]`, so its induced mixed set has exactly the two displayed
positive fibers, each of area one half. Thus `M=1`. The two shapes
are not translates, so this is not a product with a common continuous
fiber, even after an affine regression shear.

The conditional centers are `g_0=(1/3,1/3)` and `g_1=(2/3,1/6)`.
Regression on the binary base fits these two centers exactly. Hence
the residual covariance is the equally weighted average of the two
conditional covariances:

`Sigma_0=(1/144)[[8,-4],[-4,8]]`,
`Sigma_1=(1/144)[[32,-4],[-4,2]]`,
`Sigma=(1/144)[[20,-4],[-4,5]]`.                        (6)

The minimum feasible normalized cap budget is `2/9`, and it is
attained with six covariance-normalized caps: three isolated canonical
centroid vertex caps on each fiber.

Every six-cap cover at that budget has this canonical structure. A
cap containing a fiber centroid must use area at least `2/9` in that
fiber. Equality forces a canonical vertex cap, by the previously
proved simplex equality classification, and leaves zero cap mass on
the other fiber. Caps that miss a centroid miss a neighborhood of it.
To cover all points sufficiently near that centroid, all three
canonical types are necessary: if one type is missing, moving a
little from the centroid toward that vertex avoids the other types.
There are only six caps, so exactly three belong to each fiber.

On either fiber the simultaneous inequalities for those three local
canonical caps force the unique contact to be its centroid. Other
fiber caps are strictly negative there. Therefore every saddle contact
measure is supported on that centroid and assigns weight only to
local caps.

For a cap belonging to base zero, the mass and base equations imply
`r_i S_{i,1}=0`: its actual cap mass and contact mass both have base
mean zero, while any other-fiber section mass has base one. The
corresponding statement holds at base one by subtraction from the
mass equation. Thus no multiplied section force on the other fiber
can alter (5), even if the cap plane supports that other fiber.

Now take the cap of `K_0` directed toward `(1,0)`, with
`beta=(1,0)`. Its normalized normal, mass, and hinge are

`u=(6/sqrt(5),0)`, `c=2/9`, `Psi=8/[27 sqrt(5)]`.

Its cap-centroid displacement is `(2/9,-1/9)`. Directly from (6),

`c(g_cap-g_0)=(4/81,-2/81)`,
`Psi Sigma u=(4/81,-4/405)`.

The second coordinates differ by `-2/135`. Consequently (1) cannot
hold with a positive objective multiplier. Every sharp-budget
Fritz--John system for this six-cap fixed-source problem is abnormal,
even under residual-covariance normalization.

The same obstruction applies to the unframed six-cap whole-space
cover class: its canonical families cover all continuous space and
have the same unique contacts. No assertion is made about appending
additional fixed-normal frame caps, changing the cap count, or a
body-variation problem in which the covariance itself changes.
